notes: If the village casts you out the night before a contest, the show no longer fizzles with 'no one left to take' while your old neighbors stand right there. The System recasts from the living at Haven — the show must go on, and now it's personal.

The first contest the System ever airs is now its pilot episode — it says so out loud, apologizes for the jank in advance, and stumbles over your names exactly once. The countdown, the arena, and the stakes are completely real: this is a test broadcast, not a rehearsal.

Small honesty pass on the death sequence: a villager accused of two things at once is mourned once, not twice in a row — and old unfinished conversations pick up without repeating themselves mid-sentence.
After a death, the village remembers who it was talking to: villagers pick up unfinished threads naming your predecessor — nobody pretends the new face was in the room.

Promises the dead bearer made are released, not dumped on you: favors they were asked come back as honest re-asks, and the trust a distrusted bearer held no longer conjures free standing for their successor.
Overnight deaths name their cause honestly now: starving in the night says starvation, not "the night".
Village gossip reads like people talking: mangled sentences fixed, and nobody repeats the same rumor three times in one sitting.
When someone's bursting to tell you news, they tell you the thing they opened with — the treeline sighting doesn't fizzle into gossip.
Promises hold their shape: saying "count me in" twice doesn't earn double trust, and a casual "I can't" after you've already said yes doesn't make them act betrayed.

Sleep finally listens to the game's own advice: drink and eat before bed and you wake restored. The wrung-out morning is back to meaning you went to bed truly empty — not that the night quietly drank your water.
The people in the big story beats are people you actually know now: the System's arrival and the homecoming moments speak through real villagers from your roster, not strangers.

Conversations wrap up on their own now: when someone's out of steam they say so and get back to their day, instead of talking in circles until you walk away. A good thread still gets its one last beat first.
People remember your promises straight: a favor you said you'd do comes back up as the promise it was — nobody thanks you for things you haven't done yet.
Drinking at a creek or spring now drinks the water in front of you — no bottle required, one honest sip at a time. Bottles are for carrying water home.
Your pack finally has a Drink button: the water you haul is drinkable anywhere, not just standing at the shore.

Rage and Cornered Rat do what their cards say now: Rage hits harder for your next three strikes after you unleash it — no more free double damage just for holding it while hurt. Cornered Rat only kicks in when you're genuinely surrounded by three or more enemies, and the extra dodge it promised is real.

Every beast now has a trick — a lateral counter you learn by doing, not by grinding stats. Sidestep the bulldozer's lane, wound the hushwolf lead, shout down the belltoad chorus, buy off the lockpick with food. Pull it off mid-fight and the codex records it for good.

The village learns together: once Haven has killed enough of one kind of beast, asking around teaches you its trick. And every carcass leaves a hint in the Monster Codex — the kill teaches, even when brute force won.
Known tricks pay: killing a beast whose counter you've learned counts double toward opening the next wave.
Fat game butchers honestly now: bears, boars and javelinas yield their meat plus slabs of separable fat (render it over a fire) — the same animal, nothing conjured from thin air.
Reaching into a box trap is the dangerous part again: a rattlesnake in the box means pinning it behind the head first, the way the trapping knowledge always warned. The careless take the bite.

The fishing line now catches what's actually in the water: fished-out creeks stay quiet until they recover, catches carry the real species' weight, and pond fish run small like the copy always promised.
Old traps from older saves rot away cleanly at dawn instead of breaking the morning.

Three more wave-3 monsters fight the way their stories always said they would. The Callback wears the face of someone your village lost — it speaks in their voice, using things they actually said, and fights with their moves. Hold a funeral for them mid-fight — say goodbye properly — and it lets go. Or look it in its too-symmetrical eyes and tell it what it isn't.

Buffering lives three seconds in the past: it tells you exactly what it will do next, and it means it. Its afterimages are the lie — the faintest frame is where it really is. Stand perfectly still and it swings at where you were going to be. Or close your eyes and swing at where it IS.

The Ad Break pauses the whole fight for a sponsored message — a real progress bar, and it heals while you watch. Wait for the skip button (it comes sooner if the audience loves you), look away and starve it of attention, or pop the little sponsor-creature riding the glyph to fast-forward.

Three of the Final Draft’s monsters finally fight the way their stories always said they would. The Redactor points at something you love — your weapon, your footing, even your last turn — a full round before it redacts it into silence; carry a decoy rattle and it takes the loudest thing instead, or go quiet for two turns and it starves.

Gavel holds a real trial: it accuses you from your own history, waits a round, then the verdict falls. You can object (costs fame), demand a recess (once), or confess first (smaller verdict — but everyone remembers). Flank it; frontal attacks hit the sound-block.

The Focus Group rates your every move out loud — loved actions hit harder but get answered, hated ones are safe but weak. Pop its three mouth-heads to end it, or just be boring for three rounds and they’ll wander off.

Three of the Final Draft's monsters fight for real now. The Spool tapes your opening moves and plays them back at you — feed it something harmless (a wait, a bandage) and its replay is useless. The Chorus Line keeps a 4/4 beat you can hear coming — dance through the downbeat, move with it, flank it, or break its rhythm with a handful of gravel. And the Terms of Service will try to get you to sign mid-fight — read the fine print; there's a way out in section zero.

Alien players stay dead now. Kill one and they're gone for good — no more running into the same hunter weeks later sending you packages from beyond the grave. The feed marks the moment with a silence, then the betting resumes.
They've also stopped gloating about kills they didn't make: beat one in a fight and they react like someone who lost, and a dead hunter gives no post-fight speech.

Late-wave monsters now bite through armor the way they were always meant to: the Final Draft's claws find seams, the Mirror Draft's teeth find more, and the Producers barely notice plate at all. Armor still helps — it just isn't a wall anymore past wave 3.

The ground remembers now: forage the same turf too hard and it thins — lush to picked-over to barren. Examine or work a patch to read its state; rested ground comes back, but it takes weeks, not days.
You can farm at the haven: clear a plot, sow seeds from plants you actually know, tend it daily, harvest every few days. A kept garden feeds people. A neglected one dies.
Your neighbors work the same ground. Shared turf thins faster — and they notice. Talk it out at their fire (split the territory, pay tribute, or threaten them), or let it fester into raids.
Fishing got stronger: creeks always hold fish, and a skilled fisher who reads the water sometimes doubles up on the line.
